name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,345

entries.clue: Developing adoration about French wine and golf (8)

indicatorNotes.about: A thing turned about faces the way it came, so the word before it is written from its last letter back.

blocks.note: adoration is love, turned round to run the other way
vin is the French word for wine, wanted here in French rather than in translation
golf is G in the NATO alphabet radio operators spell with

annotation.surface: A growing fondness for French red and a round on the course.
annotation.walkthrough: Golf is the radio alphabet's G rather than the game, and the clue asks for 'French wine' because it wants the French word itself, not a claret.
annotation.definitionFit: Both words name gradual change over time: a plan that is evolving is a plan developing, one stage growing out of the last.

entries.clue: Italian city uprising stopped by a leader (7)

indicatorNotes.uprising: An uprising rises, and in a down entry rising means climbing the column, so those letters are written upwards.
indicatorNotes.stopped by: Something stopped by a thing has that thing planted in its way, so the letters break apart to let it in.

blocks.note: the Italian city is Rome, set to run up the column
per means a, the sense in twice a day or five pounds a head

annotation.surface: A riot in an Italian city being put down by the man in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A' is the shortest word in the clue and the one carrying letters: per is a, as in sixty miles an hour. The city looks like scenery and is the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An emperor rules an empire and the kings inside it, the highest rank a ruler holds, so 'leader' is the plain category word for him.

entries.clue: Lecture’s nothing to value (5)

blocks.note: nothing is a nought, written as the letter O
to value something is to rate it

annotation.surface: A dismissive verdict that the talk held nothing worth valuing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lecture' is the verb here, the thing a speaker does, not the noun the sentence offers. The apostrophe-s only joins the halves; it carries no letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To orate is to hold forth formally to an audience, which is what a speaker does to lecture them — the same act, one register up.

entries.clue: Very strangely end civility in spiteful manner (12)

indicatorNotes.strangely: Something done strangely comes out other than it should, so the letters around it are not left in the order they were given.

blocks.note: very is V, as in the V important letters of a memo
anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: Politeness coming to a strange end, and nastily with it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very' reads as an intensifier for 'strangely' and is a letter of the fodder instead — which is why the count comes out one short if you miss it.
annotation.definitionFit: Vindictively is the adverb for acting out of vengeful spite, so it replaces the adverbial phrase 'in spiteful manner' word for word.

entries.clue: Negative responses about society features (5)

indicatorNotes.about: What is written about a subject goes round it, so the word before opens up and closes over the letter that follows.

blocks.note: the noes are the votes against, the plural of no
S is society, the S of high society

annotation.surface: People voting against a motion on the state of society.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About society' reads as the topic of the debate and is an instruction about where one letter goes. The plural definition is the tell that the negative responses are plural too.
annotation.definitionFit: The nose is the most prominent of the features on a face, so the plural picks them out by their place rather than by a synonym.

entries.clue: Nasty smell socks discharged is to dominate (4)

indicatorNotes.discharged: Socks discharged have been emptied of everything they held, so the word keeps only its outside letters and loses its middle.

blocks.note: BO is body odour, the playground's nasty smell
the two outside letters of 'socks', the middle emptied out

annotation.surface: Foul-smelling socks finally being got rid of.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discharged' reads as dismissal in the picture and means emptied in the instruction. BO is one of the shortest pieces a setter can hand over, so the smell is always worth checking.
annotation.definitionFit: To boss someone is to order them about and have your way with them, which is to dominate them.

entries.clue: Take bulbous vegetable cut by Greek character (7)

indicatorNotes.cut by: A vegetable cut by a knife falls open where the blade goes in, so the word splits and holds what cut it.

blocks.note: the bulbous vegetable of the kitchen is an onion
pi is a Greek letter, and 'character' here means a letter rather than a person

annotation.surface: An onion being sliced by somebody from Greece.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take' is the noun of 'my take on it', not the verb the sentence opens with — a one-word definition doing its best to look like the start of an order.
annotation.definitionFit: Your take on a matter is your opinion of it, the informal noun both words share.

entries.clue: Child in class progressing (5)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in something lies inside it, so the letters wanted sit unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: an unbroken run starting on the last letter of 'class' and stopping four letters into 'progressing'

annotation.surface: A child moving up through the school year.
annotation.walkthrough: The run starts on the last letter of a word, which is where hidden words hide best — the eye reads 'class' whole and never stops on its final S.
annotation.definitionFit: Sprog is British slang for a kid, borrowed from forces slang for a raw recruit, so 'Child' is the plain word behind it.

entries.clue: Crucial worker supporting a factory set up on harbour (3,9)

indicatorNotes.set up: Something set up has been stood on its end, and in a down entry that means its letters are written from the bottom upwards.
indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry one thing on another rests above it, so the piece named first sits over the piece named second.
indicatorNotes.supporting: A worker supporting something holds it up from underneath, so those letters go below everything else.

blocks.note: the article is taken as itself, a single letter
a factory is a mill, stood on end so it climbs the column
a harbour is a port
the crossword's worker is the ant, the insect that never stops

annotation.surface: A workman propping up a factory that has been put up beside the harbour.
annotation.walkthrough: Worker is the ant, a convention worth owning outright — it turns up in every other puzzle. 'Set up' only means a turnaround because this is a down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Something all-important matters above everything else around it, which is what 'Crucial' says: the one thing a plan turns on.

entries.clue: Simple aircraft, reportedly (5)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: What comes reportedly comes by ear rather than in writing, so the word beside it is wanted for its sound and spelt another way.

blocks.note: an aircraft is a plane, and said aloud that noise has a second spelling in English

annotation.surface: Word reaching us that the aircraft in question was a basic one.
annotation.walkthrough: Two spellings share one sound and the clue tells you which end to start from: the meaning wanted is the first word, the noise is the second.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain means unadorned or straightforward — plain food, plain speaking — which is the sense 'Simple' carries.

entries.clue: Comparatively smooth type that is welcomed by senior (7)

indicatorNotes.welcomed by: Whoever welcomes a guest takes them inside, so the senior's letters open up and close round what came before.

blocks.note: Sr is senior, the tag printed after a father's name when his son shares it
a type or sort is an ilk, as in others of that ilk
ie is Latin id est, 'that is', the abbreviation used in writing

annotation.surface: A smooth sort of man being made welcome by an older colleague.
annotation.walkthrough: Two abbreviations sit either side of 'ilk' in a seven-letter answer, so almost every letter comes from a word too small to look like fodder. 'Type' is the innocent-looking one.
annotation.definitionFit: Silkier is the comparative of silky, smooth to the touch or to the ear, so 'Comparatively smooth' asks for exactly the -er form.

entries.clue: Deer groomed regularly (3)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed step through the word, here every second one, counting from the second.

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'groomed'

annotation.surface: A deer that gets brushed down on a schedule.
annotation.walkthrough: Four words make a whole picture, which is why the instruction reads as scenery. Counting from the second letter rather than the first is the reading 'regularly' usually wants.
annotation.definitionFit: The roe is the small deer of British and European woodland, usually called the roe deer, so 'Deer' names its kind.

entries.clue: Stimulating and popular group of secret agents, we’re told (9)

indicatorNotes.we’re told: What we are told arrives by ear, so the words before it are wanted for the noise they make rather than their spelling.

blocks.note: what is popular is in, in fashion
a group of secret agents is a spy ring, and said aloud the two words run together into one string of letters

annotation.surface: Word reaching us of a well-liked network of spies.
annotation.walkthrough: The sound wanted is a whole two-word phrase, not a single word, so it has to be heard across the gap between them. 'Popular' is in, the shortest piece in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Something inspiring stirs you into feeling or action, which is what 'Stimulating' names, and both are adjectives in the same -ing form.

entries.clue: Refund on returned electronic tablet (6)

indicatorNotes.returned: Something returned goes back the way it came, so the words after it are written from their last letter to their first.

blocks.note: re means on, in the sense of on the subject of — the re at the head of a memo
electronic is E and a tablet is a tab; run together and sent back they read this way

annotation.surface: Money promised on an electronic tablet sent back to the shop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returned electronic tablet' is a complete shop story, and only its first word is an instruction. Re for 'on' is the memo heading, the sense in 're your letter of the 5th'.
annotation.definitionFit: A rebate is money handed back on something already paid for, which is a refund.

entries.clue: Waiting to get new cover for book (7)

indicatorNotes.to get: A word that gets something takes it in and keeps it, so the waiting letters open up to hold the new one.

blocks.note: to be waiting is to be biding, as in biding your time
N is new, the N of a product label

annotation.surface: Holding on until a new jacket arrives for the book.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Biding' survives almost nowhere except 'biding your time', so 'Waiting' does not look like a word with a synonym hiding in it. New is the crossword's N.
annotation.definitionFit: A book's binding is the sewn or glued casing that holds its pages together and makes its cover, so the definition points at the physical thing.

entries.clue: Love to write ER’s first episode (6)

blocks.note: love is nothing on a tennis scoreboard, written as the letter O
to write something is to pen it
the italics mark the hospital drama's title, handed over as the two letters it is spelt with

annotation.surface: A fond look back at the first episode of the hospital drama ER.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics are the clue's way of saying those two letters stand as they are, a title rather than a word. 'Love' is the tennis scorer's nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: The opener is the first item in a run of them — the first episode of a series, the first match of a season.

entries.clue: Alleged grass retains position (7)

indicatorNotes.retains: What retains a thing keeps hold of it inside, so the grass closes round the letters that follow.

blocks.note: a reed is the tall grass of riverbanks and marshes
to position something is to put it somewhere

annotation.surface: A suspected police informer keeping hold of his job.
annotation.walkthrough: Grass is British slang for an informer, which is the sense the whole surface leans on; the wordplay wants the plant. 'Position' is a verb here, not the job he keeps.
annotation.definitionFit: A reputed expert is one said to be so without proof, which is exactly the doubt 'alleged' carries about anything it describes.

entries.clue: One overhauls tank in Nevada city with soldiers (9)

annotation.definitionNote: 'One overhauls' stands for 'one who overhauls': crosswords routinely drop the relative pronoun, so a verb phrase does duty for the noun naming whoever does it.

indicatorNotes.in: A thing in a place sits inside it, so the tank drops in among the letters the rest of the clue supplies rather than joining on the end.

blocks.note: Reno is the gambling city of northern Nevada
a tank for holding liquid is a vat
OR is Other Ranks, the British army's soldiers below officer rank

annotation.surface: Someone servicing a tank in a Nevada city, with troops standing by.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tank' is the brewery sort, though the soldiers alongside work hard to suggest the armoured one. OR ends a great many answers and is worth learning early.
annotation.definitionFit: A renovator does up a house or a machine — overhauls it — so the definition describes the job rather than naming the trade.

entries.clue: King and kids avoiding motorway services (5)

indicatorNotes.avoiding: Kids avoiding the motorway keep well clear of it, so the letter standing for motorway is left out of the word.

blocks.note: R is rex, Latin for king, the letter a monarch signs after their name
small children are mites
M is motorway, from the M1 and the M6, and this is the letter dropped from the word above

annotation.surface: A king and some children steering clear of the motorway services.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Motorway services' is the roadside stop with the petrol and the burgers, and the clue needs those two words prised apart. M for motorway is the M of M1.
annotation.definitionFit: A rite is a prescribed form of ceremony, so the services held in a church — matins, a funeral, a wedding — are its rites.

entries.clue: Tropical fish both sides of the craft going north (5)

indicatorNotes.both sides of: Both sides of a word are its two outside letters, with whatever stands between them left behind.
indicatorNotes.going north: North is up the map, and in a down entry up the column runs against the way the answer is written, so those letters are reversed.

blocks.note: the outside letters of 'the', its middle dropped
craft is art, the skill of doing a thing, sent up the column

annotation.surface: A fish keeping to both sides of a boat as it heads north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The' is fodder, which is why the sentence reads so smoothly — nobody suspects an article of carrying letters. Craft is skill, not the vessel the fish swims past.
annotation.definitionFit: Tetras are the small, bright freshwater fish of South American rivers that fill heated home tanks, so 'Tropical fish' is the trade's name for them.

entries.clue: Element of cappuccino on counter? (3)

indicatorNotes.Element of: An element of a thing is one part of it, so a part of the word that follows is taken — an unbroken run of its letters.
indicatorNotes.on counter: To run counter to something is to run against it, so the letters found are read the other way about.

blocks.note: an unbroken run inside 'cappuccino', starting on its fourth letter
the run is then read backwards, which is what turns it into a word

annotation.surface: A cappuccino standing on the café counter.
annotation.walkthrough: Read straight through, the whole clue describes the thing itself, and the question mark is apologising for how loosely. 'Counter' is the café's counter in the picture and 'against' in the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Read as one sentence the clue describes a cup: the part of a cappuccino you actually pick up, standing on the counter where it was served.

entries.clue: Church of Ireland ignoring female vocal group (5)

indicatorNotes.ignoring: To ignore something is to leave it out, so the letter standing for female is dropped from what has been assembled.

blocks.note: CH is church, as printed on an Ordnance Survey map
the little word is taken as it stands, both its letters
F is female, as ticked on a form, and this is the letter struck out
Ir is the dictionary's short form for Ireland and Irish

annotation.surface: A church in Ireland that will not let women sing.
annotation.walkthrough: The Church of Ireland is the Anglican church there, and the clue hands you its name to spell straight out rather than a phrase to decode — one letter too many, until 'ignoring' takes one back.
annotation.definitionFit: A choir is the body that sings together in a church or a concert hall, so 'vocal group' names it by what it is for.

entries.clue: Person with siblings allowed on outing (7)

indicatorNotes.on: In an across entry a thing laid on another is reached after it, so the word named first is written second.

blocks.note: an outing is a trip
to allow something is to let it happen

annotation.surface: Somebody being allowed along on a day out with their brothers and sisters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' is the only instruction in the clue and it works backwards: along a row, the piece named first ends up second. 'Allowed' hides LET, a chunk so common it stops registering.
annotation.definitionFit: A triplet is one of three children born at the same birth, so each one is a person with siblings — two of them, exactly.

entries.clue: Choose personal trainer following fuss (5)

indicatorNotes.following: What follows a thing comes along behind it, so the trainer's letters are written after the fuss rather than before.

blocks.note: a fuss is an ado, as in much ado about nothing
PT is the gym's personal trainer, and the army's physical training too

annotation.surface: Picking a personal trainer after a great deal of bother.
annotation.walkthrough: PT reaches crosswords through physical training, the school timetable's name for games, which is why it is worth knowing beyond the gym.
annotation.definitionFit: To adopt a plan or a policy is to choose it and take it up as your own.

entries.clue: Son to get older wise person (4)

blocks.note: S is son, the abbreviation used on a family tree
to get older is to age

annotation.surface: A son growing old and growing wise with it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To get older' is the verb age, not the noun, and the infinitive is what keeps the two halves reading as one sentence about a family.
annotation.definitionFit: A sage is someone of deep and settled wisdom, the elder people come to for counsel, which is what 'wise person' says.

entries.clue: Rum crated up and secured (8)

indicatorNotes.Rum: Rum is British for odd or peculiar, as in a rum do, and letters called odd are not in the order they should be.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A consignment of rum boxed up and made safe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rum' is the drink in the picture and the signal in the clue, British slang for odd. 'Up' looks like part of the instruction and is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An army that has captured a town has secured it — taken it and holds it — so the two past participles cover the same act.
